title: Step 13: Audit history: database trigger vs application events, and the trade-offs
summary: A row trigger records every change from every writer as a jsonb diff, with the user named per transaction through set_config. Application events record intent but only from code that remembers to write them. TraceLite keeps the trigger and lets the service label its changes.

examples.title: Migration 006: one trigger function, the actor from set_config, diffs as jsonb

annotations.note: One table for the history of requirements, test cases and links. Test runs aren't audited: they are insert-only evidence already, and step 2's RESTRICT keeps them.
now() is the transaction's start time, the same for every row it writes. xact (pg_current_xact_id, PG 13) groups those rows, so the UI can show "one save changed these four things".

No foreign key, unlike everything else in TraceLite. Step 2's question, whether the child is part of the parent or a record about it, has the second answer here: the record of a deleted project must survive the delete. row_id has no foreign key either, which is why the history at the end outlives AUTH-RESET.
to_jsonb(OLD) and to_jsonb(NEW) make one function work for every table. The timestamps are dropped: the audit row has its own, and an updated_at in every diff would hide what really changed.
The diff keeps only the members whose values differ, each as [old, new]. A save that changed nothing but updated_at produces no row, so the history shows edits, not clicks on Save.

The user comes from a setting the application puts in the transaction. current_setting with missing_ok true returns NULL if it was never set, but '' once any transaction on this connection has set it (example 3), hence nullif. Without a user, the database login stands in, marked db:.
The bridge between the two designs: the service may name what it is doing (move, import), and the trigger stores that label next to the facts.

AFTER ROW triggers on the audited tables. On the same table and event, triggers fire in alphabetical order of their names, so requirements_audit runs before step 9's requirements_notify; both belong to the same transaction.
trace_links has no id; TG_ARGV names the column that identifies the row in the history, and a link belongs to its requirement's.

set_config(name, value, is_local true) is SET LOCAL as a function: it takes the value as a parameter, and it ends with the transaction. Store.WithTx sends it first in every transaction (example 3). This runner keeps the whole script in one transaction, so each "request" below sets its own values.
A move, labelled by the service. Moving is just a parent_id change to the database; the label is what makes "moved under AUTH-LOGIN" readable in the history.
The same title saved again: at most updated_at differs, which the function ignores, so it returned without a row. Three UPDATEs, two entries in the history.
One DELETE, and the foreign key's cascade removed the link too. Both rows are recorded under Ayşe's name: a cascade runs as ordinary row deletes, triggers included.

The detail page's history: the full row for an insert or a delete, [old, new] pairs for updates. The link's rows appear because their row_id is the requirement, and all of it is still there after the requirement is gone.

examples.title: The same changes, recorded by a trigger and by application events: what each one misses

annotations.note: The rows exist before the trigger does, so both designs start with zero records.
Example 1's function without the label and the timestamp handling: the user, the code, and for an UPDATE the members that changed, as [old, new].

The application-events design: the service inserts one row per use case, in the same transaction as the change (step 11's outbox idea), with names a person can read: kind, the code at the time, and the parts of the change that matter.
After each step, mark stores how many records each design holds. A step that a design missed leaves its number where it was.
A use case through the service: both designs record it, the trigger as a diff, the service as an event.
A fix in psql, or a migration's data fix, is plain DML: the trigger records both rows, under the login role; the service never ran, so its log has nothing.
ADD COLUMN with a constant default fires nothing at all: since PG 11 the default is kept in the catalog, and no row is written.
Both designs live in the transaction, so both lose the attempt when it rolls back. Recording failed attempts means writing outside the transaction, which then also records things that never happened.
TRUNCATE removes rows without firing ON DELETE row triggers. An ON TRUNCATE statement trigger could record that it happened, not what was removed.
The tally: the trigger missed only what bypasses DML (DDL, TRUNCATE); the service missed every write that didn't go through it.

The same move, twice. The trigger knows the fact (parent_id went from one uuid to another); the event knows the meaning (moved from AUTH to AUTH-LOGIN), with codes, which stay readable after the requirement is deleted.

examples.title: Naming the user through a connection pool: session settings leak, transaction settings don't

annotations.note: The one place where the user reaches the database. Every store method that writes runs inside WithTx, so every audited write carries a user; a single autocommitted statement outside it would not.
A bind parameter, so a user name can't change the SQL. SET has no parameters; people who use it build the statement with Sprintf.
One connection makes the reuse certain. With a pool of 4 under load, the same thing happens to some requests, which is worse: the wrong name appears only sometimes.
The trigger in this example reports what it would record as a notice (the schema is at the end); pgx hands every notice to this function, so each record prints under the request that made it.
After WithTx commits, the setting is gone: the next write, from a path that named no one, is recorded as db:playground, a visible gap instead of a wrong name.
The setting now exists on this connection with the value '', not NULL, which is why the trigger wraps it in nullif.

The tempting version: SET names the user for the session. The setting stays on the connection after Ayşe's request returns it to the pool, and the next request's change is booked to her. Undoing it on every release (pgxpool has an AfterRelease hook) is a rule that must never be forgotten; a transaction-local setting needs no cleanup.

use_cases: Change history on a detail page: who changed the title, when, from what to what
Compliance questions (who approved this requirement, who removed that link) that must be answered for writes from psql, imports and migrations too
Attributing changes in a pooled-connection application without a database role per user
Deciding, for any cross-cutting record (audit, notifications, search indexing), whether the database or the application should produce it
strengths: The trigger sees every row written by INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, COPY and cascades, from any client: a forgotten code path shows up as a db: entry instead of a hole
Diffs are computed from OLD and NEW, so they are exact; an application event says what the code believed it changed
set_config(…, true) scopes the user to one transaction, which is the right lifetime with a connection pool; SET would leak to the next borrower
Audit rows commit and roll back with the change, so the log never claims a change that didn't happen
weaknesses: A row trigger runs once per row: a 10,000-row import writes 10,000 audit rows in 10,000 function calls; statement-level triggers with transition tables would batch them
The trigger records facts, not intent: a move is a parent_id change between two uuids until the service labels it
DDL, TRUNCATE, disabled triggers and session_replication_role = replica bypass it, and a table owner can disable it
Nothing records attempts that rolled back, in either design

pitfalls.title: SET instead of set_config(…, true) on a pooled connection
pitfalls.detail: A session-level setting outlives the request and is seen by the next one that borrows the connection, so its changes are attributed to the previous user. Set the user transaction-locally, first thing in every transaction.

pitfalls.title: Testing current_setting(…, true) only for NULL
pitfalls.detail: Once a custom setting has been set on a connection, it exists there with the value '' after the transaction ends, and missing_ok no longer returns NULL. Treat '' as unset.

pitfalls.title: Writes outside the transaction helper
pitfalls.detail: A single statement sent through the pool, outside WithTx, runs in its own transaction where nobody set the user. Route every write through the helper, and treat db: entries in the log as bugs to find.

pitfalls.title: Auditing with BEFORE triggers
pitfalls.detail: A BEFORE trigger runs before constraints are checked and before later BEFORE triggers may change the row, so it can record values that are never stored. Audit in AFTER triggers, which see the row as written.

pitfalls.title: Copying secrets into the log
pitfalls.detail: to_jsonb(NEW) copies every column. Don't attach the generic trigger to tables like webhooks, whose secret would end up in the history; or remove such members in the function.

quiz.q: TraceLite's pool has 4 connections. A middleware runs SET tracelite.actor = <user> once per request. What goes wrong?
options: A later request on the same connection that doesn't set the user is recorded under the previous user's name
quiz.why: SET lasts for the session, which outlives the request; set_config(…, true) ends with the transaction.

quiz.q: A bulk load COPYs rows straight into requirements. Which design records them?
options: Only the trigger: COPY FROM fires row triggers
quiz.why: COPY FROM invokes the table's triggers and constraints; with application events, the loader would need to write its own event.

quiz.q: A migration runs ALTER TABLE requirements ADD COLUMN priority int NOT NULL DEFAULT 3. What does the audit trigger record?
options: One row for the whole table
quiz.why: DDL fires no row triggers, and a constant default is stored in the catalog rather than written into each row.

quiz.q: Why does the audit_log have no foreign key to projects?
options: The history must survive the project's deletion
uuid columns can't have foreign keys
quiz.why: It is a record about the project, not part of it; with CASCADE it would vanish, with RESTRICT no project could ever be deleted.

body:
## Concept

The question "who changed this requirement, and what did it say before?" has two honest
answers.

**A database trigger** (migration 006). An `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE … FOR EACH
ROW` trigger on `requirements`, `test_cases` and `trace_links` writes one `audit_log`
row per changed row, with the diff as jsonb. The database doesn't know TraceLite's
users, so the application tells it: the first statement of every transaction is
`set_config('tracelite.actor', $1, true)`, and the trigger reads it back with
`current_setting`.

**Application events.** The service writes a `change_events` row for each use case
(`requirement.moved`, `requirement.renamed`) in the same transaction as the change, with
the user it already knows and the data a person wants to read.

They fail differently:

| | Trigger | Application events |
|---|---|---|
| Writes through the service | yes, as diffs | yes, as named use cases |
| Rows removed by a foreign key's `ON DELETE CASCADE` | yes, each one | only what the use case names |
| psql fixes, bulk SQL, migrations' data fixes | yes, user shown as `db:<role>` | no |
| COPY, and step 7's import (COPY to staging, then INSERT … SELECT) | yes: COPY FROM fires row triggers | only if the importer writes one |
| DDL (`ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT`), `TRUNCATE` | no | no |
| Rolled-back transactions | no (rolled back with them) | no (same) |
| Intent ("moved under AUTH-LOGIN") | only if the service labels it | yes |

TraceLite keeps the trigger as the record of what happened, because a history that
misses whole categories of writes can't answer an auditor. It borrows the one strength
of events: the service may label a change (`set_config('tracelite.action', 'move',
true)`), and the trigger stores the label next to the diff.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java/Hibernate Envers, Spring Data auditing**: entity listeners write revisions,
  which is the application-events design generated for you. They see what goes through
  the ORM, and nothing else. `@CreatedBy` comes from an `AuditorAware` bean, usually
  reading Spring Security's thread-local context; here the user travels in the
  `context.Context` and then in the transaction.
- **Python/django-simple-history, Rails/PaperTrail**: same model, same blind spots
  (`queryset.update()` in Django skips save signals, `update_all` in Rails skips
  callbacks). A trigger can't be skipped by choosing a different API call.
- **JS/Prisma middleware or extensions**: the same again, per client instance.
- **Change data capture (Debezium, logical decoding)**: reads the WAL, so it sees
  every committed change, like the trigger, without slowing the writer. It runs as a
  separate service and still can't name the application user unless the application
  writes it somewhere: the same problem `set_config` solves here.

## How it works

`migrations/006_audit.sql` is example 1's middle part. The store side, in
`internal/store/store.go`:

```go
// WithTx: step 3's helper; the actor comes from the request's context.
return pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, s.db, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
	if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx, "SELECT set_config('tracelite.actor', $1, true)", ActorFrom(ctx)); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return fn(s.q.WithTx(tx))
})
```

`ActorFrom` reads what a middleware put into the request's context. In a single-user
local install that is the owner's name from configuration (step 15); with
authentication, the signed-in user. A use case that wants a label sets
`tracelite.action` the same way inside its closure (`move` for moves, `import` for step
7's importer).

Bulk loads need nothing extra. PostgreSQL's COPY reference says that `COPY FROM` invokes
the destination table's triggers and check constraints, so a pgx `CopyFrom` inside
`WithTx` is recorded row by row under the loading user. Step 7's importer copies into a
staging table and then runs `INSERT … SELECT` into `requirements`, which the trigger sees
like any other insert.

The history endpoint, in `openapi.yaml`:

```yaml
  /api/requirements/{requirementId}/history:
    parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/RequirementId" }]
    get:
      operationId: getRequirementHistory
      parameters: [{ $ref: "#/components/parameters/Limit" }, { $ref: "#/components/parameters/Cursor" }]
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Newest first, keyset-paged by id
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                required: [items, nextCursor]
                properties:
                  items:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: object
                      required: [at, actor, action, table, op, changes]
                      properties:
                        at: { type: string, format: date-time }
                        actor: { type: string }
                        action: { type: string }
                        table: { type: string, enum: [requirements, test_cases, trace_links] }
                        op: { type: string, enum: [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE] }
                        changes: { type: object }   # the full row, or {column: [old, new]}
                  nextCursor: { type: [string, "null"] }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/Problem" }
```

It reads `audit_log` by `row_id` through `audit_log_row`, so it works for deleted
requirements too, as long as the client still has the id. The keys inside `changes` are
column names, snake_case, because they describe the table and not the wire format; the
detail page maps the few it shows (`title`, `status`, `parent_id`) to Turkish labels.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as Handler
  participant S as Store.WithTx
  participant P as PostgreSQL
  H->>S: MoveRequirement(ctx with actor "mehmet")
  S->>P: BEGIN
  S->>P: SELECT set_config('tracelite.actor', 'mehmet', true)
  S->>P: SELECT set_config('tracelite.action', 'move', true)
  S->>P: UPDATE requirements SET parent_id = ...
  P->>P: requirements_audit: INSERT INTO audit_log (actor mehmet, action move, diff)
  P->>P: requirements_notify (step 9): pg_notify, queued until commit
  S->>P: COMMIT (both, or neither)
```

## Design notes

**Same choice as step 9, different weights.** Step 9 chose a trigger for change
notifications because every writer must notify, and a lost or extra notification costs
only a refetch. For the audit trail the "every writer" argument is stronger still (a
history with holes is worse than none, because it is believed), and the cost of the
trigger's weakness, missing intent, is softened by the action label. If TraceLite's
history were mainly a product feature ("Ayşe moved this under AUTH-LOGIN") rather than a
record, application events would win, and a trigger could still backstop them.

**Row triggers and bulk writes.** A row trigger costs one function call and one insert
per changed row. For TraceLite's imports (thousands of rows, rarely) that is acceptable.
At larger scale, statement-level triggers with transition tables (`REFERENCING OLD TABLE
AS … NEW TABLE AS …`) write the whole statement's audit rows in one `INSERT … SELECT`;
the price is one trigger per event, because a trigger with transition tables can't be
attached to several events at once.

**What the trigger can't stop.** A table owner can `ALTER TABLE … DISABLE TRIGGER`, and
`session_replication_role = replica` disables ordinary triggers for a session (it needs
superuser or a granted SET privilege). The application's role owns the tables (it runs
the migrations), so an attacker with its password could bypass the audit. A stricter
setup migrates with an owner role, runs the application as a role without ownership, and
grants it only INSERT on `audit_log`: then the application can't rewrite history either.
TraceLite, installed on one machine for one team, doesn't go that far; it says so in its
installation notes.

**Retention.** Audit rows are small, but they are never updated and rarely read.
Requirements change slowly enough that years of history fit easily; if a project ever
needed limits, a range partition per year (sql.modeling.temporal) lets old years be
detached and archived without a `DELETE`.
